stimuli.text: A block of mass 5 kg on a 30° incline is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass 7 kg. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.2. The system is released from rest, and the hanging block descends.
A block of mass 0.5 kg on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring. Its position is $$x(t) = 0.07\cos(12t)$$, with x in meters and t in seconds.
Students measure the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths, using small amplitudes.
A hoop (I = MR²) and a solid sphere (I = ⅖MR²) of equal mass M and radius R are released from rest at the top of the same ramp of height 2.9 m. Both roll without slipping.

questions.stem: Masses of 10 kg and 2 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley. What is the magnitude of their acceleration?

options.why: The masses are connected, so a is less than g.
The fraction is inverted.
Correct. a = (m₁ − m₂)g/(m₁ + m₂).
The whole system accelerates: divide by both masses.

questions.stem: A 0.9 kg mass oscillates on a spring with $$k = 55$$ N/m. What is the period?

options.why: Correct. T = 2π√(m/k).
The ratio is m/k.
That is the frequency.
Include the 2π.

questions.stem: An oscillator's position is $$x(t) = 0.16\cos(3t)$$ m. What is its maximum acceleration?

options.why: That is v_max.
Multiply by the amplitude.
Correct. a_max = Aω².
Differentiate twice: Aω².

questions.stem: A 3 kg cart moving at 7 m/s collides with and sticks to a 7 kg cart at rest. What is their speed after the collision?

options.why: Kinetic energy is not conserved here.
Use m₁v₁ for the initial momentum.
The carts share the momentum.
Correct. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.

questions.explanation: v_f = 3·7/10 = 2.1 m/s; kinetic energy lost = 51.5 J.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 0.9 m swings about a pivot at one end with small amplitude. What is its period?

options.why: d is L/2, the distance to the center of mass.
A rod is a physical pendulum, not a simple one.
I = mL²/3.
Correct. T = 2π√(I/(mgd)) with I = mL²/3 and d = L/2.

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 90 kg load 14 m at constant speed in 18 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: Correct. P = mgh/t.
Include g.
P = W/t.
That is the work; divide by time.

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 2x^2$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 2$$ m to $$x = 4$$ m?

options.why: The force is not constant.
Divide by n + 1 when integrating.
Correct. W = ∫F dx.
Integrate; do not just evaluate F.

questions.stem: A particle's position is $$x(t) = 4t^3 + 2t^2 + 1t$$, with x in meters and t in seconds. What is its velocity at $$t = 3$$ s?

options.why: That is the position; differentiate it.
Bring each exponent down as a factor when differentiating.
Correct. Differentiate once: v = 3at² + 2bt + c.
The constant term c is part of the velocity.

questions.explanation: v(t) = 12t² + 4t + 1, so at t = 3 the value is 121.

questions.stem: A wheel spinning at 45 rad/s slows uniformly to rest in 18 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

options.why: The average angular speed is ω₀/2.
Recheck the average.
Correct. Δθ = ½ω₀t, then divide by 2π.
That is in radians; convert to revolutions.

questions.stem: A planet has 4 times Earth's mass and 4 times Earth's radius. What is the gravitational field strength at its surface? (Earth's is 9.8 N/kg.)

options.why: g depends on 1/R², not 1/R.
g decreases with radius.
The ratio is inverted.
Correct. g ∝ M/R².

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 2x^3 - 15x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: dU/dx = 3ax² − b.
Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.
Take the square root.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 6x² − 15 = 0 gives x = 1.58 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 270$$ N/m is compressed 0.17 m and launches a 1 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: Take the square root.
Use energy: v = x√(k/m).
The ½ appears on both sides.
Correct. ½kx² = ½mv².

questions.stem: A 81 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating upward at 3 m/s². What does the scale read?

options.why: Include gravity.
Check the direction of the acceleration.
Correct. The scale reads the normal force: N − mg = ma (up positive).
The acceleration changes the normal force.

questions.stem: A boat points straight across a river 120 m wide, moving at 6 m/s relative to the water. The current flows at 1 m/s. How long does the crossing take?

options.why: Correct. The current does not change the time to cross; it only carries the boat downstream.
The current is perpendicular to the heading.
The perpendicular component alone sets the crossing time.
The current is perpendicular to the heading.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 0.8 m is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration just after release?

options.why: The weight acts at L/2.
Use τ = Iα with I = ML²/3.
τ = MgL/2.
Correct. τ = Mg(L/2) and I = ML²/3 give α = 3g/(2L).

questions.stem: A rod lies along the x-axis from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 5$$ m and has linear mass density $$\lambda = kx^2$$. Where is its center of mass?

options.why: Correct. x_cm = ∫xλ dx / ∫λ dx.
The exponents are n + 2 and n + 1.
The rod is not uniform.
Integrate x·xⁿ and xⁿ correctly.

questions.stem: A constant torque of 11 N·m acts on a wheel ($$I = 0.2$$ kg·m²) initially at rest, through 3 revolutions. What is the wheel's final angular speed?

options.why: W = ½Iω².
½Iω² = W; solve for ω.
Correct. Work τΔθ (in radians) equals ½Iω².
Convert revolutions to radians.

questions.stem: A 0.4 kg ball hits a wall at 18 m/s and rebounds at 9 m/s. The contact lasts 0.07 s. What is the average force from the wall?

options.why: Include the rebound.
The velocity reverses, so the speeds add.
Correct. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) with the direction reversed.
Divide by time.

questions.stem: A car rounds a flat curve of radius 30 m. The coefficient of static friction is 0.6. What is the maximum speed without skidding?

options.why: Take the square root.
Include the friction coefficient.
μ multiplies g r.
Correct. Static friction supplies the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r.

questions.stem: A 2500 kg car heading east at 15 m/s collides with a 500 kg car heading north at 12 m/s, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?

options.why: Divide by the total mass.
Momentum is a vector; add components at right angles.
Weight each velocity by its mass.
Correct. Conserve momentum in x and y separately, then combine.

questions.stem: A 5 kg ball moving at +8 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 8 kg ball at rest. What is the velocity of the 8 kg ball afterward (positive in the original direction)?

options.why: Only equal masses exchange velocities.
Correct. Elastic: conserve momentum and kinetic energy (relative velocity reverses).
That would be a sticking collision.
Kinetic energy is conserved too.

questions.explanation: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = -1.85 m/s; v₂' = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 6.15 m/s.

questions.stem: A solid cylinder rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 2.4 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ½MR².
Some energy goes into rotation.
Rotational energy is ½Iω² = ½βmv².
That is only correct for a hoop.

questions.stem: A 2 kg ball on a 0.9 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the bottom of the circle its speed is 8 m/s. What is the tension in the string there?

options.why: Check the direction of gravity relative to the center.
Include gravity.
Centripetal force uses v².
Correct. At the bottom, T − mg = mv²/r.

questions.stem: A car moving at 22 m/s brakes with a constant deceleration of 2 m/s². How far does it travel before stopping?

options.why: Correct. Use v² = v₀² + 2aΔx with v = 0.
Δx = v₀²/(2a).
That is the stopping time in seconds.
Divide by 2a, not a.

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 3x$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 1$$ m to $$x = 3$$ m?

options.why: Correct. W = ∫F dx.
Integrate; do not just evaluate F.
The force is not constant.
Divide by n + 1 when integrating.

questions.stem: A block slides down a 25° incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.1. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?

options.why: Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
The component along the incline is mg sin θ.
Friction acts up the slope.
Correct. a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ).

questions.stem: A 4 kg object at rest experiences a net force $$F(t) = 8t^2$$ N from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 4$$ s. What is its final speed?

options.why: Correct. Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum.
Integrate the force over time.
The force is not constant.
Divide by the mass to get speed.

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 6 m down a 30° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².
Friction removes energy.
Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.

questions.explanation: h = 3 m. v = √(2g(h − μL cos θ)) = 5.31 m/s.

questions.stem: An object's acceleration is $$a(t) = 5t$$ m/s². At $$t = 0$$ it has velocity 3 m/s and is at $$x = 0$$. What is its position at $$t = 5$$ s?

options.why: Integrating tⁿ divides by n + 1.
Include the initial velocity.
Correct. Integrate twice, using the initial conditions.
That is the velocity.

questions.stem: Satellite B orbits a planet in a circular orbit 2 times the radius of satellite A's circular orbit. What is the ratio of B's orbital period to A's?

options.why: Kepler's third law: T ∝ r^(3/2).
Correct. T² ∝ r³, so T ∝ r^(3/2).
T² ∝ r³.
The exponent is 3/2.

questions.stem: A uniform 5 m beam weighing 500 N rests on supports at both ends. A 700 N load sits 3 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?

options.why: Include the beam's weight at its center.
The load is not at the center.
Correct. Take torques about the left support.
That is the left support's force.

questions.stem: A 6 kg block on a horizontal table is connected by a string over a light pulley to a hanging 2 kg block. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the table and the block is 0.2. What is the acceleration of the blocks?

options.why: Include friction on the table block.
Both blocks accelerate; divide by the total mass.
Correct. Net force (m₂g − μm₁g) divided by the total mass.
Divide by the total mass.

questions.stem: A mass on a spring oscillates with angular frequency 8 rad/s and amplitude 0.14 m. What is its speed when it is 0.084 m from equilibrium?

options.why: That is the maximum speed, at x = 0.
Speed is greatest at equilibrium, not at the ends.
Use A² − x² under a square root.
Correct. v = ω√(A² − x²), from conservation of energy.

questions.stem: An object of mass 0.9 kg falls from rest with a drag force $$F = -bv$$, where $$b = 0.09$$ kg/s. What is the time constant of its approach to terminal speed?

options.why: τ = m/b.
Correct. From m dv/dt = mg − bv, τ = m/b.
That is the terminal speed.
τ has units of seconds: m/b.

questions.explanation: v_T = mg/b = 98 m/s and τ = m/b = 10 s.

questions.stem: A ball is launched from level ground at 24 m/s at 30° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, what is its maximum height?

options.why: Use the vertical component, v₀ sin θ.
H = (v₀ sin θ)²/(2g).
Correct. Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately.
Only the vertical component matters.

questions.explanation: v₀x = 20.8 m/s, v₀y = 12 m/s. H = v₀y²/(2g) = 7.35 m.

questions.stem: A 3 kg mass hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass 4 kg that turns on a frictionless axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?

options.why: For a disk, I/R² = M/2.
I/R² = M/2.
Correct. a = mg/(m + M/2), using I = ½MR² and a = Rα.
The pulley's inertia reduces the acceleration.

questions.explanation: mg − T = ma and TR = ½MR²(a/R) give a = 5.88 m/s².

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 7 kg and radius 0.2 m rotates about an axis perpendicular to it, 0.5 m from its center. What is its rotational inertia?

options.why: The parallel-axis term is Md².
Correct. Parallel-axis theorem: I = ½MR² + Md².
Include the disk's own I about its center.
The axis is not through the center.

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$8 \times 10^{24}$$ kg and radius $$1 \times 10^{7}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: Correct. ½mv² = GMm/R.
Take the square root.
Potential energy uses 1/R.
That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.

questions.stem: A constant torque of 12 N·m acts on a wheel ($$I = 0.1$$ kg·m²) initially at rest, through 4 revolutions. What is the wheel's final angular speed?

options.why: ½Iω² = W; solve for ω.
Correct. Work τΔθ (in radians) equals ½Iω².
W = ½Iω².
Convert revolutions to radians.

questions.stem: A 21 g bullet moving at 250 m/s embeds in a 1.4 kg block hanging from strings. How high does the block rise?

options.why: Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision.
Correct. Momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing.
h = V²/(2g).
Find the block's speed after the collision first.

questions.explanation: V = 3.69 m/s after the collision; h = V²/(2g) = 0.696 m.

questions.title: Block on an incline with a hanging mass

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a free-body diagram for the 5 kg block, labeling each force.

rubric.criterion: Weight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, tension up the incline.
Kinetic friction down the incline (opposite the motion).

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system in terms of the masses, θ, μ and g, then calculate its value.

rubric.criterion: Newton's second law applied to each block (or the system).

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string.
Calculate the speed of the blocks after the hanging block has descended 2 m, and the work done by friction on the incline block during that motion.

rubric.criterion: Work by friction, with a negative sign.

parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) graphs of position, velocity and acceleration versus time for one period, aligned vertically.

rubric.criterion: Position is a cosine starting at +A; velocity is a negative sine starting at 0.
rubric.example: x starts at 0.07 m; v starts at 0 and goes negative.

rubric.criterion: Acceleration starts at its negative maximum and is opposite in sign to position throughout.

parts.prompt: Derive expressions for v(t) and a(t), and determine the maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
Calculate the spring constant and the period.
Calculate the total mechanical energy and describe how kinetic and potential energy vary during one period.

rubric.example: K is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; U is the reverse; the sum is constant. Each varies twice per period.

parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to measure the period accurately, including how to reduce uncertainty.

rubric.example: Time 10 swings with a stopwatch and divide by 10.

rubric.criterion: Keep the amplitude small and repeat trials.
rubric.example: Release from under about 10° and average several trials.

parts.prompt: Identify quantities to graph that would give a straight line, and explain how g can be found from the graph.
Plot (describe) the linearized data and draw a best-fit line. Use it to calculate an experimental value of g.
The students repeat the experiment with a much larger amplitude. Predict how the measured periods would change and explain.

rubric.criterion: Periods increase slightly; the small-angle approximation (sin θ ≈ θ) no longer holds.
rubric.example: The restoring torque is less than proportional to θ at large angles.

parts.prompt: Without calculating, predict which object reaches the bottom first. Justify your prediction using energy.

rubric.example: It has the smaller rotational inertia per MR².

rubric.criterion: Justification: less of its energy goes into rotation, so more is translational kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed at the bottom of an object with rotational inertia βMR², in terms of g, h and β.

rubric.criterion: Energy conservation including both forms of kinetic energy, with v = Rω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of each object at the bottom.
Explain whether your derived expression is consistent with your prediction in part (a), and why neither speed depends on M or R.

rubric.criterion: Smaller β gives larger v, consistent with the prediction.
M and R cancel in the energy equation.
rubric.example: Only the shape factor β matters.
